note: Geometry is a public GrabCAD quadcopter sample standing in for a real AXOM airframe. Every canonical key below was read from the converted GLB with cad-pipeline/inspect_glb_nodes.mjs, never typed from the raw CAD names — see docs/MEMORY.md for the two runtime name-rewriting rules that makes necessary. All `website` figures are illustrative placeholders, not specifications.

9Fan#20.description: Counter-clockwise lift rotor on the front-left arm. The motor stator is fixed to the arm boom; the propeller, spinner and retaining nut turn together as one rigid body.

specs.label: Rotating / fixed
specs.note: Verified separable in the CAD — this is what makes RPM control possible.

specs.label: Blade pitch
specs.note: Both blades are one watertight solid with no separable mesh island, so a rigid pitch is geometrically impossible here.

9Fan_1#52.description: Clockwise lift rotor on the front-right arm, mirroring Rotor 1. Opposing rotation across the diagonal is what cancels yaw torque on a quadrotor.

specs.label: Rotating / fixed
specs.note: Verified separable in the CAD — this is what makes RPM control possible.

specs.label: Blade pitch
specs.note: Both blades are one watertight solid with no separable mesh island, so a rigid pitch is geometrically impossible here.

9Fan_2#53.description: Counter-clockwise lift rotor on the rear-right arm. Differential thrust between this rotor and its diagonal pair produces pitch and roll authority.

specs.label: Rotating / fixed
specs.note: Verified separable in the CAD — this is what makes RPM control possible.

specs.label: Blade pitch
specs.note: Both blades are one watertight solid with no separable mesh island, so a rigid pitch is geometrically impossible here.

9Fan_3#54.description: Clockwise lift rotor on the rear-left arm. Each rotor is a fixed-pitch two-blade propeller, so thrust is modulated by shaft speed alone.

specs.label: Rotating / fixed
specs.note: Verified separable in the CAD — this is what makes RPM control possible.

specs.label: Blade pitch
specs.note: Both blades are one watertight solid with no separable mesh island, so a rigid pitch is geometrically impossible here.

4Spider_Arm#13.description: Truss-braced arm carrying the front-left rotor. The open truss geometry is what keeps arm mass down without giving up bending stiffness at the motor mount.

4Spider_Arm_1#49.description: Truss-braced arm carrying the front-right rotor.

4Spider_Arm_2#50.description: Truss-braced arm carrying the rear-right rotor.

4Spider_Arm_3#51.description: Truss-braced arm carrying the rear-left rotor.

1_Spider_Base#1.description: Primary structural plate. All four arms, the landing standoffs and the power distribution stack land on this one part, so it carries every flight load into the airframe.

2_Spider_top#14.description: Closes the frame sandwich above the avionics bay and provides the battery mounting face.

3Distribution_Board#0.description: Splits the battery feed to the four electronic speed controllers and provides regulated rails for the avionics.

3Distribution_Board_1#6.description: Second distribution layer, stacked above the first to keep high-current and signal wiring on separate planes.

11Battery#67.description: Lithium-polymer pack carried on the upper plate. Battery mass dominates the all-up weight, so its position sets the airframe's centre of gravity.

12Electrical_Unit#7.description: Inertial measurement and control unit. Mounted inboard and low, where rotor-induced vibration is smallest.

13_Electrical_Unit_2#8.description: Command link and telemetry downlink electronics.

7Electrical_Connector#55.description: Electronic speed controller driving the front-left rotor. Commutation frequency is what the flight controller varies to change rotor thrust.

7Electrical_Connector_1#58.description: Electronic speed controller driving the rear-left rotor.

7Electrical_Connector_2#59.description: Electronic speed controller driving the front-right rotor.

7Electrical_Connector_3#60.description: Electronic speed controller driving the rear-right rotor.
